module_title: Gupta Empire and Harsha - Economy, Decline, Feudalism, and Inscriptions
introduction: At this advanced level, we will deeply analyze the causes of the Gupta Empire's decline (like Huna invasions), the rise of feudalism originating from land grants, intricacies of the economy, and historical inscriptions.

core_concepts.title: Land Grants and the Rise of Feudalism
core_concepts.description: During the Gupta and Harsha periods, the practice of granting tax-free land (Agrahara) to Brahmins and temples increased significantly, leading to the rise of feudalism and a weakened central authority.

core_concepts.title: Huna Invasions
core_concepts.description: The Hunas, a Central Asian tribe, repeatedly attacked the Gupta Empire. Skandagupta successfully repelled them initially, but continuous attacks shattered the empire's economy.

core_concepts.title: Gupta Economy and Trade
core_concepts.description: Trade with the West declined after the fall of the Roman Empire, but trade with Southeast Asia grew. The Guptas issued the largest number of gold coins (Dinar), though their purity was lower than those of the Kushanas.

core_concepts.title: Prayag Prashasti (Allahabad Pillar Inscription)
core_concepts.description: Composed by Harishena, this inscription is the most authentic source of Samudragupta's military campaigns. It is engraved on the same Ashokan pillar that also bears Jahangir's inscription.

core_concepts.title: Aihole Inscription
core_concepts.description: Composed by Ravikirti, this inscription details how Chalukya king Pulakeshin II defeated Harshavardhana on the banks of the Narmada, halting his southern expansion.

important_entities.name: Skandagupta
important_entities.significance: The Bhitari Pillar Inscription describes his victory over the Hunas.

important_entities.name: Pulakeshin II
important_entities.significance: The only ruler who successfully stopped Harshavardhana's military campaigns.

important_entities.name: Harishena
important_entities.key_fact: Court poet and Sandhi-Vigrahika of Samudragupta
important_entities.significance: Composed the Prayag Prashasti, an excellent example of the Champu style (mixed prose and poetry).

important_entities.name: Dinar and Rupayaka
important_entities.significance: Dinars were gold coins, and Rupayaka were silver coins issued by Chandragupta II after defeating the Shakas.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.alert_title: Quantity vs. Purity of Gold Coins
trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: The Guptas issued the 'highest number' of gold coins (Dinars), but the 'purest' gold coins were issued by the Kushanas.
It is often associated with the Vedic period, but the first archaeological evidence of the Sati system is found in the 'Eran Inscription' (510 CE, Bhanugupta) of the Gupta period.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Aihole Inscription relates to the battle between Harsha and Pulakeshin, while Bhitari Pillar Inscription relates to Skandagupta and the Hunas.

exam_strategy_tips: UPSC and State PCS exams frequently feature analytical (statement-based) questions on the socio-economic impacts of 'Land Grants' and the resulting feudalism.
Rote-learn the various inscriptions (Prayag Prashasti, Aihole, Mehrauli Iron Pillar, Eran) along with their composers and associated rulers.
